dx: Alcoholic cirrhosis with gynecomastia and testicular atrophy
case: A 56-year-old man comes to the physician because of enlargement and tenderness of both breasts for 6 months and decreased libido. He has consumed about 10 alcoholic drinks daily for 30 years. Physical examination shows scleral icterus, spider angiomas over the upper chest, palmar erythema, shifting dullness, and a tender, rubbery, 3-cm disc of tissue beneath each areola. Each testis measures about 8 mL (15 to 25). Laboratory studies show albumin 2.6 g/dL (3.5 to 5.0), total bilirubin 3.1 mg/dL (0.1 to 1.2), INR 1.8 (0.9 to 1.1), estradiol 64 pg/mL (10 to 40), and total testosterone 270 ng/dL (300 to 1000). Diagnosis: alcoholic cirrhosis with gynecomastia and testicular atrophy.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the spider angiomas and palmar erythema in this patient?
options: Estradiol secretion by the adrenal zona reticularis
Reduced renal filtration of unbound estradiol
Impaired hepatic inactivation of estrogens
Increased secretion of prolactin by the pituitary
approach: Link spider angiomas and palmar erythema to excess estrogen effect, which also fits the high estradiol and the gynecomastia.
Recall that the liver inactivates estrogens by conjugating them to glucuronides and sulfates for excretion in bile and urine.
A failing liver clears estrogens poorly, so their levels and effects rise.
questions.why: The liver normally inactivates estradiol and estrone by conjugating them to glucuronides and sulfates, which are then excreted in bile and urine. In cirrhosis this clearance falls, so estrogen levels and estrogen effects rise. Estrogen dilates small skin vessels, which produces spider angiomas on the upper body and redness of the palms. The same excess drives gynecomastia and suppresses LH, which adds to the testicular atrophy caused by alcohol itself.
whyNot: The zona reticularis secretes weak androgens such as DHEA, with little estradiol. Adrenal estrogen excess occurs only with rare feminizing adrenal tumors.
Estrogens are excreted mainly after conjugation in the liver. Kidney filtration of unbound hormone is a minor route, and this patient has no sign of kidney failure.
Correct.
High prolactin can cause galactorrhea and hypogonadism, but it does not dilate skin vessels. Spider angiomas and palmar erythema point to excess estrogen effect.

questions.stem: His 63-year-old brother, who carries a pathogenic BRCA2 variant, is concerned about breast cancer. Which of the following findings on breast examination in a man most strongly suggests carcinoma rather than gynecomastia?
options: Hard eccentric mass fixed to the overlying skin
Tender rubbery disc centered beneath the areola
Enlargement of both breasts over several months
Soft tissue that grew after starting a new medication
approach: Recall that gynecomastia is a benign proliferation of ducts and periductal stroma driven by a high estrogen to androgen ratio.
It grows outward from beneath the nipple, is often bilateral, and is often tender while growing.
Carcinoma is usually unilateral, hard, painless, off center from the nipple, and may tether the skin or retract the nipple.
questions.why: Gynecomastia forms a soft to rubbery disc centered under the areola, often in both breasts, and it is commonly tender while it grows. Male breast carcinoma usually presents as a single hard, painless mass that sits off center from the nipple and may be fixed to the skin or cause nipple retraction or bloody discharge. Men with a BRCA2 mutation or Klinefelter syndrome have the highest risk of male breast carcinoma. Gynecomastia itself is not considered a precursor of carcinoma.
whyNot: Correct.
A tender, rubbery disc centered under the areola is the classic finding in gynecomastia, as in this patient.
Bilateral enlargement over months favors gynecomastia. Male breast carcinoma is almost always unilateral.
Onset after a drug such as spironolactone points to drug-induced gynecomastia from a raised estrogen to androgen effect.

questions.stem: His serum sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) concentration is 96 nmol/L (10 to 57). Which of the following best explains this finding and its effect on his androgen status?
options: Androgen excess raising SHBG, raising free testosterone
Low albumin raising SHBG, raising free testosterone
Estrogen excess raising SHBG, preserving free testosterone
Estrogen excess raising SHBG, lowering free testosterone
approach: Recall that testosterone circulates bound tightly to SHBG, loosely to albumin, and only about 2% free.
Estrogen raises hepatic SHBG production; androgens, insulin resistance, and obesity lower it.
More SHBG binds more testosterone, so the free, active fraction falls further than the total level suggests.
questions.why: Estrogen stimulates the liver to make SHBG, and SHBG is typically high in cirrhosis. SHBG binds testosterone more tightly than estradiol, so a high SHBG lowers free testosterone more than free estradiol. This tilts the balance further toward estrogen effect and adds to his gynecomastia, low libido, and testicular atrophy. His measured total testosterone underestimates how low his active hormone is.
whyNot: Androgens lower SHBG production, and this patient has low testosterone. A higher SHBG level would also lower the free fraction.
Low albumin does not raise SHBG. A rise in SHBG binds more testosterone, which lowers the free fraction.
When SHBG rises, more testosterone is bound and the free fraction falls. Free testosterone is not protected.
Correct.

questions.stem: A testicular biopsy shows small seminiferous tubules with few germ cells. The tubules are lined mostly by tall cells that reach from the basement membrane to the lumen and are joined to each other near the base by tight junctions. In a healthy testis, these cells perform which of the following functions?
options: Secretion of testosterone into the interstitial capillaries
Secretion of androgen-binding protein into the tubule lumen
Rhythmic contraction that moves sperm toward the rete testis
Presentation of antigen to T cells in the interstitium
approach: Identify the cells: tall cells that span the epithelium and join by basal tight junctions are Sertoli cells.
Their tight junctions form the blood-testis barrier.
Under FSH, Sertoli cells make androgen-binding protein, which holds testosterone at high levels in the tubule lumen, and inhibin B.
questions.why: Sertoli cells are the supporting cells of the seminiferous epithelium. Tight junctions between neighboring Sertoli cells form the blood-testis barrier, which shields developing germ cells from the immune system. Under FSH, Sertoli cells secrete androgen-binding protein into the lumen, which keeps testosterone concentrated where spermatogenesis needs it, and inhibin B, which feeds back on FSH. Sertoli cells survive when germ cells are lost, so atrophic tubules are lined mostly by them.
whyNot: Leydig cells in the interstitial tissue between the tubules secrete testosterone in response to LH. They do not line the tubules.
Correct.
Peritubular myoid cells contract to move sperm and fluid toward the rete testis. They are flat cells outside the basement membrane.
Interstitial macrophages handle antigens between the tubules. They are not joined by tight junctions inside the tubule.

dx: Menopause with genitourinary syndrome of menopause
case: A 54-year-old woman comes to the physician because of vaginal dryness, pain with intercourse, and burning with urination for 1 year. Her last menstrual period was 18 months ago, and she has had hot flashes and night sweats since then. She takes no medications. Her body mass index is 22 kg/m2. Pelvic examination shows a pale, thin, smooth vaginal mucosa with loss of rugae and scattered petechiae. Vaginal pH is 6.0 (3.8 to 4.5). Urinalysis shows no leukocytes or nitrites. Serum FSH is 86 mIU/mL (follicular phase 3.5 to 12.5), and estradiol is below 15 pg/mL. Diagnosis: menopause with genitourinary syndrome of menopause.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains this patient's vaginal pH?
options: Less epithelial glycogen to support lactobacilli
Overgrowth of Candida species in the thinned vaginal wall
Increased alkaline mucus secretion by endocervical glands
Reflux of alkaline urine from the bladder into the vagina
approach: Link the timing: the vaginal changes followed the loss of ovarian estradiol at menopause.
Estrogen keeps the vaginal epithelium thick and rich in glycogen.
Lactobacilli turn glycogen breakdown products into lactic acid; with little glycogen they decline and the pH rises.
questions.why: Estradiol makes the vaginal epithelium proliferate and store glycogen in its superficial cells. Lactobacilli use the glycogen breakdown products to make lactic acid, which keeps vaginal pH at about 4.5 or lower. After menopause the epithelium becomes thin and glycogen-poor, lactobacilli decline, and the pH rises above 5. The thin, dry mucosa explains her pain with intercourse, and estrogen loss in the urethra and bladder lining explains her urinary burning with a normal urinalysis.
whyNot: Correct.
Candida vaginitis is more common in high-estrogen states such as pregnancy, and it leaves the pH at 4.5 or lower. It causes itching and a thick white discharge.
Endocervical mucus production depends on estrogen and falls after menopause.
Urine does not reflux into the vagina in a woman with normal anatomy, and her urinalysis is normal.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the predominant circulating estrogen in this patient and its main source?
options: Estradiol from residual ovarian granulosa cells
Estriol from hepatic hydroxylation of estradiol
Estradiol from testosterone in the endometrium
Estrone from androstenedione in adipose tissue
approach: After menopause the follicles, and the aromatase in their granulosa cells, are gone.
The adrenal cortex and ovarian stroma still release androstenedione.
Aromatase in adipose tissue converts androstenedione to estrone, which becomes the main postmenopausal estrogen.
questions.why: Before menopause, granulosa cells convert theca cell androgens to estradiol, the main estrogen. After the follicles are exhausted, estradiol falls sharply. The adrenal cortex and ovarian stroma still secrete androstenedione, and aromatase in adipose tissue converts it to estrone. Estrone is a weaker estrogen, and a lean woman like this patient makes little of it, so her estrogen effect is low. Women with more adipose tissue make more estrone, which slows bone loss but raises the risk of endometrial hyperplasia when no progestin opposes it.
whyNot: Granulosa cells line the developing follicles. Once the follicles are depleted at menopause, this source largely disappears.
Estriol is the main estrogen of pregnancy, made by the placenta from fetal adrenal DHEA sulfate. It is a minor estrogen in nonpregnant women.
Normal endometrium is a target of estrogen and has little aromatase activity. Testosterone is also a minor substrate compared with androstenedione.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her 29-year-old daughter has had no menses for 6 months after previously regular cycles. A pregnancy test is negative. Serum studies show FSH 2.1 mIU/mL (follicular phase 3.5 to 12.5), LH 1.6 mIU/mL (follicular phase 2.4 to 12.6), estradiol 18 pg/mL (follicular phase 30 to 120), prolactin 11 ng/mL (less than 25), and TSH 1.9 microU/mL (0.5 to 4.5). MRI of the pituitary is normal. Which of the following is the most likely site of the daughter's disorder?
options: Ovarian follicle pool
Hypothalamic GnRH neurons
Basal layer of the endometrium
Pituitary lactotrophs
approach: Pregnancy, thyroid disease, and hyperprolactinemia are excluded by the normal results.
Low estradiol shows the ovary is either understimulated or unable to respond; the gonadotropins decide which.
Low FSH and LH with low estradiol place the defect above the ovary, and a normal pituitary MRI points to the hypothalamus.
questions.why: An ovarian cause would remove estradiol and inhibin feedback, so FSH would be high, as in her mother at menopause. Here FSH and LH are low even though estradiol is low, so the ovary is not being stimulated. With normal prolactin, normal TSH, and a normal pituitary, the most likely cause is reduced pulsatile GnRH release, as in functional hypothalamic amenorrhea from stress, weight loss, or heavy exercise. An outflow problem such as Asherman syndrome would leave all hormone levels normal.
whyNot: Loss of the follicle pool removes negative feedback and raises FSH, as in menopause or primary ovarian insufficiency.
Correct.
Damage to the basal endometrium (Asherman syndrome) stops bleeding but leaves FSH, LH, and estradiol normal.
A lactotroph adenoma would raise prolactin, which is normal here.

questions.stem: She also reports a bulge at the vaginal opening when she strains. During her first delivery she had a deep midline perineal tear that healed poorly. Pelvic examination shows a short distance between the vaginal opening and the anus, and the lower posterior vaginal wall bulges outward on straining. Damage to which of the following structures best explains these findings?
options: Uterosacral ligament
Round ligament of the uterus
Perineal body
Broad ligament
approach: Locate the injury: a midline tear between the vagina and anus passes through the perineal body.
The perineal body is the fibromuscular center of the perineum, where the bulbospongiosus, transverse perineal muscles, external anal sphincter, and fibers of the levator ani attach.
Loss of this anchor weakens support of the lower posterior vagina and perineum.
questions.why: The perineal body is a mass of fibromuscular tissue between the vaginal opening and the anus. Several perineal muscles and part of the levator ani attach to it, so it anchors the lower vagina. A deep midline tear that heals poorly shortens and weakens it, and the lower posterior vaginal wall can then bulge outward, often with the rectum behind it. The cardinal and uterosacral ligaments support the cervix and upper vagina instead, so their weakness lets the uterus descend.
whyNot: The uterosacral ligaments hold the cervix and upper vagina back toward the sacrum. A midline perineal tear does not reach them.
The round ligament keeps the uterus tilted forward and runs through the inguinal canal. It gives little support against prolapse.
Correct.
The broad ligament is a peritoneal fold that carries vessels to the uterus and adnexa. It provides little mechanical support.

dx: Primary ovarian insufficiency from autoimmune oophoritis in a woman with Addison disease
case: A 31-year-old woman comes to the physician because she has had no menses for 7 months and has hot flashes and night sweats. Menarche was at age 12, and her cycles were regular until this year. Two years ago she was diagnosed with primary adrenal insufficiency, and she takes hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone. A pregnancy test is negative. Serum FSH is 64 mIU/mL (follicular phase 3.5 to 12.5) on two occasions 4 weeks apart, and estradiol is 14 pg/mL (follicular phase 30 to 120). Prolactin and TSH are within the reference ranges. Karyotype is 46,XX, and FMR1 testing is normal. Antibodies to adrenal cortex are present. Diagnosis: primary ovarian insufficiency from autoimmune oophoritis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains how a single autoimmune process caused both her adrenal failure and her ovarian failure?
options: Autoimmunity to the zona pellucida of the oocyte
Autoimmunity to FSH receptors on granulosa cells
Autoimmunity to gonadotrophs of the anterior pituitary
Autoimmunity to steroidogenic enzymes in both glands
approach: Note the pairing: primary adrenal insufficiency and ovarian failure in the same woman.
High FSH places the defect in the ovary itself.
The shared targets are steroid-making cells and enzymes found in both glands, such as cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme and 17-alpha-hydroxylase.
questions.why: Steroid-producing cells of the adrenal cortex and of the ovarian theca share enzymes such as cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme and 17-alpha-hydroxylase. In autoimmune polyglandular disease, T cells and steroid-cell autoantibodies attack these cells in both glands. In the ovary, lymphocytes infiltrate the theca of growing follicles, and the follicles are lost. Loss of estradiol and inhibin feedback raises FSH, the profile of primary ovarian insufficiency. Turner syndrome and FMR1 premutation, two other main causes, were excluded by testing here.
whyNot: An attack on the zona pellucida would involve only oocytes. It would not explain her adrenal failure.
Antibodies to FSH receptors would affect only the ovary and would not explain her adrenal failure.
Destruction of gonadotrophs (lymphocytic hypophysitis) would lower FSH and LH. Her FSH is high, so the defect is in the ovary.
Correct.

questions.stem: Ultrasonography shows a few small follicles in each ovary, and 4 months later she ovulates spontaneously. Which of the following best describes the meiotic stage of the cell released at ovulation and the number of functional gametes formed from one primary oocyte compared with one primary spermatocyte?
options: Prophase I; one ovum versus four sperm
Metaphase II; one ovum versus four sperm
Metaphase II; two ova versus four sperm
Telophase II; one ovum versus two spermatids
approach: Primary oocytes stay in prophase I from fetal life until the LH surge before ovulation.
At the surge, meiosis I finishes, the first polar body is extruded, and the secondary oocyte arrests again in metaphase II until fertilization.
Unequal cytoplasmic division gives one ovum per primary oocyte, while each primary spermatocyte gives four spermatids.
questions.why: Occasional ovulation happens in some women with primary ovarian insufficiency because a few follicles remain. The LH surge restarts meiosis I in the oocyte of the dominant follicle. The first polar body is cast off, and the secondary oocyte is ovulated while arrested in metaphase II. Meiosis II finishes only if a sperm enters, which also produces the second polar body. Because the polar bodies receive little cytoplasm, one primary oocyte yields one functional gamete, while one primary spermatocyte divides evenly into four spermatids.
whyNot: Prophase I is the arrest from fetal life until the LH surge. The ovulated cell has already finished meiosis I.
Correct.
Polar bodies are not functional gametes, so one primary oocyte yields one ovum.
The ovulated oocyte is arrested in metaphase II, and each primary spermatocyte gives four spermatids.

questions.stem: She later conceives by in vitro fertilization with a donor oocyte. Because her ovaries cannot make progesterone, she receives progesterone until the placenta takes over its synthesis. The placenta obtains most of the cholesterol for this synthesis by which of the following mechanisms?
options: Receptor-mediated endocytosis of maternal LDL
De novo synthesis from acetyl-CoA in trophoblast
Uptake of chylomicron remnants via apolipoprotein E
Lipoprotein lipase hydrolysis of maternal VLDL
approach: The placenta has little capacity to make cholesterol itself.
Steroid-making tissues such as the placenta and gonads take up circulating LDL through LDL receptors.
Cholesteryl esters from the endocytosed LDL are hydrolyzed in lysosomes, and the free cholesterol is moved into mitochondria for side-chain cleavage to pregnenolone.
questions.why: The syncytiotrophoblast makes large amounts of progesterone from maternal cholesterol. It takes up maternal LDL by receptor-mediated endocytosis, frees the cholesterol in lysosomes, and converts it to pregnenolone and then to progesterone. The gonads also rely mainly on LDL uptake. In the gonads, the step that limits the rate of steroid synthesis is StAR-mediated transfer of cholesterol into the mitochondria.
whyNot: Correct.
Trophoblast makes little cholesterol from acetyl-CoA, so it depends on cholesterol delivered in maternal LDL.
Chylomicron remnants are taken up mainly by the liver through apolipoprotein E receptors.
Lipoprotein lipase releases fatty acids from triglycerides in VLDL and chylomicrons. It does not supply cholesterol for steroid synthesis.

questions.stem: Before her diagnosis, she and her partner had tried to conceive for 14 months. His semen analysis and her hysterosalpingogram were normal. Which of the following best classifies and explains her infertility?
options: Ovulatory, from GnRH suppression by excess prolactin
Tubal, from scarring of the ampullary mucosa
Ovulatory, from loss of FSH-responsive follicles
Uterine, from intrauterine adhesions after curettage
approach: Sort female infertility into ovulatory, tubal, and uterine causes.
A normal hysterosalpingogram makes tubal and uterine causes unlikely.
High FSH with low estradiol and normal prolactin show the ovary has too few follicles left to respond, an ovulatory cause.
questions.why: Female infertility is grouped as ovulatory, tubal, or uterine. Ovulatory causes include polycystic ovary syndrome, hyperprolactinemia, and ovarian insufficiency. In this patient, autoimmune destruction has left few follicles, so FSH rises but the ovary cannot produce a dominant follicle regularly. Tubal causes follow scarring, usually from pelvic inflammatory disease, and uterine causes include Asherman syndrome and submucosal leiomyomas. Both would show on a hysterosalpingogram, which was normal here.
whyNot: Hyperprolactinemia causes ovulatory infertility with low or normal FSH. Her prolactin is normal and her FSH is high.
Tubal scarring, usually from earlier pelvic inflammatory disease, would show blocked or dilated tubes on hysterosalpingography.
Correct.
Intrauterine adhesions (Asherman syndrome) distort the cavity on hysterosalpingography and leave hormone levels normal.

dx: Prolactinoma with galactorrhea and secondary amenorrhea
case: A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because she has had no menses for 5 months and a milky discharge from both nipples for 2 months. Menarche was at age 13, and her cycles were regular until this year. She has mild frontal headaches and takes no medications. A pregnancy test is negative. Physical examination shows milky discharge expressible from both nipples, and visual fields are full. Serum prolactin is 165 ng/mL (less than 25), TSH is 1.8 microU/mL (0.5 to 4.5), FSH is 2.8 mIU/mL (follicular phase 3.5 to 12.5), and estradiol is 19 pg/mL (follicular phase 30 to 120). MRI shows an 8-mm pituitary adenoma. Diagnosis: prolactinoma with galactorrhea and secondary amenorrhea.

questions.stem: Her 34-year-old cousin, who takes risperidone for schizophrenia, has amenorrhea and galactorrhea with a serum prolactin of 88 ng/mL and a normal pituitary MRI. Which of the following best explains the cousin's hyperprolactinemia?
options: Stimulation of TRH receptors on lactotrophs
Blockade of D2 receptors on lactotrophs
Loss of estrogen feedback on the pituitary
Reduced renal clearance of prolactin
approach: Recall that prolactin is the anterior pituitary hormone held mainly under tonic inhibition.
Hypothalamic dopamine reaches lactotrophs through the portal veins and acts on D2 receptors to suppress prolactin release.
Risperidone blocks D2 receptors, which removes the brake; the high prolactin then suppresses GnRH.
questions.why: Dopamine from the arcuate nucleus travels down the hypophyseal portal veins and inhibits lactotrophs through D2 receptors. Anything that blocks this signal raises prolactin, including D2-blocking antipsychotics such as risperidone and masses that compress the pituitary stalk. High prolactin suppresses pulsatile GnRH release, so LH and FSH fall, the ovaries make little estradiol, and menses stop. Prolactin acting on breast tissue causes galactorrhea. For the same reason, dopamine agonists such as cabergoline lower prolactin and shrink prolactinomas like this patient's.
whyNot: TRH does stimulate prolactin release, which is why primary hypothyroidism can raise prolactin. Risperidone does not act on TRH receptors.
Correct.
Estrogen stimulates lactotrophs, so loss of estrogen would tend to lower prolactin.
Kidney failure can raise prolactin by reducing clearance, but nothing suggests kidney disease in the cousin, and risperidone acts directly on the pituitary.

questions.stem: Her 14-year-old sister began breast development at age 12 and now has Tanner stage 3 breasts and pubic hair. She has not had a menstrual period. Which of the following best describes the sister's status?
options: Primary amenorrhea that needs evaluation now
Secondary amenorrhea that needs evaluation now
Normal pubertal timing without amenorrhea
Delayed puberty from hypothalamic failure
approach: Primary amenorrhea means no menarche by age 15, or by age 13 if there is no breast development.
Secondary amenorrhea applies only after menses have begun.
The sister is 14 and began breast development at 12, so she meets neither definition; menarche usually follows thelarche by about 2 to 3 years.
questions.why: Primary amenorrhea is defined as no menarche by age 15 in a girl with normal secondary sex characteristics, or by age 13 if breast development has not started. Secondary amenorrhea is the absence of menses for 3 months in a woman who previously had regular cycles, as in this patient, and pregnancy is its most common cause. The sister started puberty on time and is only 2 years past thelarche, so a first period is still expected. She would need evaluation if she has no menses by age 15.
whyNot: She is younger than 15 and has breast development, so she does not meet the definition of primary amenorrhea.
Secondary amenorrhea requires earlier menses. The sister has never menstruated.
Correct.
Breast development at 12 is normal timing and shows that her GnRH axis has activated. Delayed puberty in a girl means no breast development by about age 13.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the cells that produce this patient's nipple discharge and the cells that push it into the ducts?
options: Luminal cells of lobular acini; myoepithelial cells around them
Myoepithelial cells of lactiferous ducts; luminal cells of acini
Luminal cells of lactiferous sinuses; areolar smooth muscle cells
Stromal fibroblasts of the lobules; luminal cells of terminal ducts
approach: Milk is made in the terminal duct lobular unit, the cluster of acini at the end of a terminal duct.
Each acinus and duct has two cell layers: inner luminal epithelial cells and outer myoepithelial cells on the basement membrane.
Luminal cells secrete milk under prolactin; myoepithelial cells contract under oxytocin to push it into the ducts.
questions.why: The terminal duct lobular unit is the functional unit of the breast. Its acini are lined by luminal epithelial cells, which make milk proteins, lactose, and lipids when prolactin is high, as in this patient. Around them is a layer of myoepithelial cells on the basement membrane, which contract to push milk into the terminal duct and toward the nipple. The terminal duct lobular unit is also where most breast carcinomas and fibroadenomas arise.
whyNot: Correct.
Myoepithelial cells are contractile and do not secrete milk. Secretion occurs in luminal cells of the acini.
The lactiferous sinuses near the nipple store and carry milk without making it. Areolar smooth muscle erects the nipple and does not empty the acini.
Stromal fibroblasts form connective tissue and do not secrete milk. The intralobular stroma is the source of the stromal part of a fibroadenoma.

questions.stem: Her adenoma is treated, and 2 years later she delivers a healthy term infant who receives intramuscular vitamin K at birth. She breastfeeds exclusively and gives the infant no supplements. Because human milk contains little of one vitamin, the infant is at greatest risk for which of the following vitamin deficiency disorders?
options: Beriberi
Pellagra
Scurvy
Rickets
approach: Human milk is rich in lactose, whey proteins, and secretory IgA but low in vitamin D and vitamin K.
Vitamin K was given at birth, which leaves vitamin D as the gap.
Vitamin D deficiency in an infant impairs calcium and phosphate absorption and bone mineralization, which causes rickets.
questions.why: Human milk provides lactose for energy, easily digested whey proteins, and secretory IgA that protects the infant's gut. It contains little vitamin D and vitamin K. The vitamin K injection at birth prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding, but vitamin D must come from sunlight or supplements. Without either, an exclusively breastfed infant can develop rickets, with poorly mineralized growth plates, bowed legs, and a rachitic rosary. For this reason, breastfed infants are given 400 IU of vitamin D daily.
whyNot: Beriberi from thiamine deficiency occurs in breastfed infants mainly when the mother is thiamine deficient, as with a diet of polished rice.
Pellagra from niacin deficiency is not a recognized risk of breastfeeding by a well-nourished mother.
Milk from a well-nourished mother supplies enough vitamin C. Infant scurvy is linked to diets of heated or processed milk lacking vitamin C.
Correct.

dx: Anovulatory abnormal uterine bleeding in an adolescent
case: A 15-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of heavy vaginal bleeding for 12 days. Menarche was at age 13. Since then, her periods have come anywhere from 3 weeks to 4 months apart, without a predictable pattern and without cramps. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. Body mass index is 21 kg/m2. She has no acne or hirsutism. A pregnancy test is negative. Hemoglobin is 10.6 g/dL (12.0 to 16.0). Platelet count, prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time, and von Willebrand studies are normal. Serum prolactin and TSH are within the reference ranges. Pelvic ultrasonography shows a normal uterus and ovaries with a 14-mm endometrium. Diagnosis: anovulatory abnormal uterine bleeding.

questions.stem: Which of the following features of this patient's history most strongly indicates ovulatory dysfunction rather than a structural uterine cause of her bleeding?
options: Bleeding heavy enough to cause anemia
Episodes of bleeding lasting more than 7 days
Cycles of unpredictable length without cramps
Normal platelet count and coagulation studies
approach: Ovulatory cycles are regular because the luteal phase lasts about 14 days and ends with a predictable fall in progesterone.
Structural lesions such as polyps, adenomyosis, and leiomyomas cause heavy or intermenstrual bleeding during otherwise regular cycles.
Irregular, unpredictable, painless bleeding points to anovulation.
questions.why: In an ovulatory cycle, the corpus luteum makes progesterone for about 14 days, and its fall triggers an orderly, predictable shed. Without ovulation, estrogen keeps the endometrium growing with no progesterone-induced secretory change, until parts of the thick, fragile lining break down at random. This gives bleeding at unpredictable intervals, sometimes heavy and prolonged. Menstrual cramps depend on prostaglandins made by secretory endometrium, so anovulatory bleeding is usually painless. Structural causes, the PALM group of the PALM-COEIN system, usually cause heavy or intermenstrual bleeding within regular cycles.
whyNot: Heavy bleeding with anemia occurs with both anovulation and structural lesions such as leiomyoma, so it does not separate them.
Prolonged bleeding occurs with both anovulation and structural causes.
Correct.
Normal coagulation studies rule out a bleeding disorder such as von Willebrand disease, the C in PALM-COEIN. They do not separate ovulatory dysfunction from a structural lesion.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why this patient does not ovulate regularly?
options: Excess prolactin suppressing GnRH pulses
Depletion of the follicles that respond to FSH
Androgen excess arresting follicle growth
No LH surge in response to rising estradiol
approach: Exclude the other causes of anovulation: prolactin and TSH are normal, there are no signs of androgen excess, and she is only 2 years past menarche.
Ovulation needs estradiol from a dominant follicle to switch the axis from negative to positive feedback and trigger the LH surge.
In the first few years after menarche this positive feedback is often immature, so follicles grow and make estradiol but no surge occurs.
questions.why: Ovulation depends on a mid-cycle LH surge. It happens when a dominant follicle keeps estradiol high (about 200 pg/mL for about 2 days), which switches the hypothalamus and pituitary from negative to positive feedback. In many girls during the first few years after menarche, this positive feedback is not yet mature. Follicles develop and make estradiol, but there is no LH surge, no corpus luteum, and no progesterone. The unopposed estrogen builds a thick endometrium, here 14 mm, which sheds irregularly and heavily. If it persists for years, unopposed estrogen also raises the risk of endometrial hyperplasia.
whyNot: Hyperprolactinemia does cause anovulation, but her prolactin is normal.
Follicle depletion (ovarian insufficiency) would cause high FSH and low estradiol with amenorrhea. Her thick endometrium shows estrogen is present.
Androgen excess, as in polycystic ovary syndrome, arrests follicle growth, but she has no acne or hirsutism.
Correct.

topics: Positive feedback and the LH surge

questions.stem: Her aunt, who has endometriosis, starts leuprolide, a long-acting GnRH agonist that keeps GnRH receptors continuously occupied. After a brief initial rise, which of the following hormone changes is expected after 4 weeks of treatment?
options: Sustained rise in LH, FSH, and estradiol
Sustained fall in LH, FSH, and estradiol
Fall in FSH with a rise in LH and estradiol
Rise in LH and FSH with a fall in estradiol
approach: GnRH is normally released in pulses, and gonadotrophs stay responsive only to intermittent stimulation.
Continuous receptor occupation first releases stored LH and FSH (the flare), then downregulates and desensitizes the GnRH receptors.
LH and FSH fall, so the ovaries make little estradiol.
questions.why: Gonadotrophs respond to GnRH pulses that arrive about every 60 to 90 minutes. Between pulses the GnRH receptors recover. A long-acting agonist occupies the receptors without a break, which first causes a flare of LH and FSH release and then receptor internalization and uncoupling. Within a few weeks LH and FSH fall, and the ovaries make little estradiol, a medical menopause. This lowers estrogen-driven growth of endometriosis. The same principle is used to suppress the axis in prostate cancer and central precocious puberty.
whyNot: A sustained rise occurs only in the first days (the flare). Continuous exposure then desensitizes the gonadotrophs.
Correct.
LH and FSH both depend on GnRH, and both fall when the receptors are desensitized.
A rise in LH and FSH with low estradiol is the pattern of ovarian failure, such as menopause, where feedback is lost.

questions.stem: Her cousin, a 15-year-old 46,XX girl, had clitoromegaly and partial labial fusion at birth, and the cousin's mother developed acne and hirsutism during that pregnancy that resolved after delivery. The cousin now has no breast development, tall stature, high serum testosterone and FSH, and very low estradiol. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes best explains these findings?
options: Aromatase
3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase
17-alpha-hydroxylase
17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase
approach: Combine the clues: virilization of both the 46,XX fetus and the mother during pregnancy, then no estrogen effect at puberty despite high androgens.
The placenta normally converts fetal and maternal androgens to estrogens using aromatase.
Without aromatase, androgens build up in mother and fetus, and at puberty the ovaries cannot make estradiol, so FSH rises and the growth plates stay open.
questions.why: Aromatase converts androstenedione to estrone and testosterone to estradiol, the last step of estrogen synthesis. In the placenta it protects mother and fetus from androgens made by the fetal adrenal. When it is absent, these androgens virilize the female fetus and the mother. At puberty the ovaries make androgens but no estradiol, so the breasts do not develop, FSH and LH rise from lost feedback, and the growth plates stay open, which gives tall stature. This patient, by contrast, makes estradiol, as shown by her thick endometrium.
whyNot: Correct.
3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency blocks cortisol, aldosterone, and sex steroid synthesis, with salt wasting in infancy. It does not cause maternal virilization.
17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency blocks androgen and estrogen synthesis, so testosterone would be low. It also causes hypertension with low potassium.
17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency lowers testosterone formation and mainly affects 46,XY development. It does not explain high testosterone with absent estradiol.

dx: Adenomyosis with dysmenorrhea and heavy menstrual bleeding
case: A 44-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 3, comes to the physician because of increasingly heavy and painful menstrual periods for 2 years. The pain begins a few days before each period and lasts through it. Two of her deliveries were by cesarean section. Pelvic examination shows a symmetrically enlarged, globular, tender uterus about the size of a 10-week pregnancy, with no discrete masses. Hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL (12.0 to 16.0), and mean corpuscular volume is 74 fL (80 to 100). A pregnancy test is negative. MRI shows diffuse thickening of the junctional zone of the myometrium. Diagnosis: adenomyosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why this patient's uterus is enlarged and tender around the time of menses?
options: Cyclic bleeding of endometrial tissue within the myometrium
Benign smooth muscle tumor nodules distorting the uterine wall
Ectopic endometrial implants on the serosal surface of the uterus
Hyperplastic endometrium filling the uterine cavity
approach: Note the uniform, globular, tender enlargement with no discrete masses.
Adenomyosis is endometrial glands and stroma deep within the myometrium, with reactive smooth muscle hypertrophy around them.
These islands respond to ovarian hormones and bleed inside the muscle each cycle, which causes pain and diffuse enlargement.
questions.why: In adenomyosis, nests of endometrial glands and stroma lie deep in the myometrium, often after uterine surgery such as cesarean delivery disrupts the boundary between endometrium and muscle. The nests respond to ovarian hormones, swell and bleed within the muscle wall during menses, and provoke hypertrophy of the surrounding smooth muscle. The uterus becomes diffusely enlarged, globular, and tender, with heavy, painful periods. Leiomyomas form discrete firm nodules instead, and endometriosis places endometrial tissue outside the uterus.
whyNot: Correct.
Leiomyomas are discrete, firm, often painless nodules that make the uterus irregular. This uterus is smooth and symmetric.
Endometriosis involves implants outside the uterus, such as on the ovaries and pelvic peritoneum. The uterus itself is usually normal in size.
Endometrial hyperplasia thickens the lining and causes abnormal bleeding, but it does not make the uterus globular and tender. MRI places the change in the myometrium.

questions.stem: Her 24-year-old daughter has regular cycles and a normal pelvic examination. Each month, about 2 weeks before her period, she has a few hours of dull pain in one lower quadrant, sometimes on the right and sometimes on the left. Which of the following best explains the daughter's pain?
options: Prostaglandin-induced contraction of the myometrium
Intermittent torsion of the ovarian pedicle
Follicle rupture with release of fluid and blood
Retrograde menstrual flow into the pelvis
approach: Time the pain: about 14 days before menses is ovulation.
Alternating sides fit whichever ovary ovulates that month.
Rupture of the dominant follicle releases fluid and a little blood that irritate the peritoneum, which causes mittelschmerz.
questions.why: Mittelschmerz is one-sided lower abdominal pain at ovulation, about 14 days before the next period. It is thought to come from stretching of the ovarian surface by the enlarging follicle and from follicular fluid and blood irritating the peritoneum when the follicle ruptures. It lasts hours to a day or two and switches sides with the ovulating ovary. Primary dysmenorrhea occurs at the start of menses instead, from prostaglandins released by the shedding endometrium.
whyNot: Prostaglandin-driven contractions cause primary dysmenorrhea, which begins with the onset of menses.
Ovarian torsion causes sudden severe pain, often with nausea and vomiting, usually in an enlarged ovary. It does not recur briefly each month.
Correct.
Retrograde menstruation occurs during menses and is a proposed cause of endometriosis, which gives pain around menses.

questions.stem: Uterine artery embolization is considered. The catheter is passed from the right common femoral artery into the left side of the pelvis. From which of the following vessels does the catheter enter the left uterine artery?
options: Abdominal aorta below the renal arteries
External iliac artery
Posterior division of the internal iliac artery
Anterior division of the internal iliac artery
approach: The uterine artery is a visceral branch of the internal iliac artery.

Visceral pelvic branches (uterine, vaginal, vesical, middle rectal, internal pudendal) come from the anterior division; the posterior division supplies the body wall (iliolumbar, lateral sacral, superior gluteal).
The uterine artery then runs medially in the base of the broad ligament and crosses above the ureter near the cervix.
questions.why: The uterine artery arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery, along with the other visceral branches of the pelvis. It runs medially in the base of the broad ligament, passes above the ureter about 2 cm lateral to the cervix, and ascends along the side of the uterus. Embolization blocks this artery to shrink adenomyosis or leiomyomas. The ovaries also receive blood from the ovarian arteries, which arise from the aorta.
whyNot: The ovarian arteries arise from the abdominal aorta just below the renal arteries. The uterine artery does not.
The external iliac artery continues as the femoral artery to the lower limb. Its pelvic branches, the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac arteries, do not supply the uterus.
The posterior division supplies the pelvic wall and gluteal region through the iliolumbar, lateral sacral, and superior gluteal arteries.
Correct.

topics: Branches of the internal iliac artery

questions.stem: Before her MRI, she also reported spotting between periods. Saline-infusion sonohysterography showed a smooth, 9-mm echogenic mass projecting from the endometrium into the cavity, with a single feeding vessel and intact underlying myometrium. Which of the following best describes this lesion?
options: Clonal proliferation of myometrial smooth muscle cells
Localized benign overgrowth of glands and stroma
Endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium
Retained placental tissue from an earlier pregnancy
approach: Locate the lesion: it arises from the endometrium and projects into the cavity, and the myometrium below is intact.
An echogenic mass with a single feeding vessel is typical of an endometrial polyp; a submucosal leiomyoma arises from the muscle and is usually hypoechoic.
Polyps are localized overgrowths of endometrial glands and stroma that bleed between periods.
questions.why: An endometrial polyp is a benign, localized outgrowth of endometrial glands and stroma, usually with thick-walled vessels in a central stalk. Polyps are fragile at the surface and cause intermenstrual or irregular bleeding. Endocervical polyps behave in the same way and are seen at the cervical os. On imaging, a polyp is echogenic and attached to the endometrium, often with a single feeding vessel, while a submucosal leiomyoma arises from the myometrium. Polyps are treated by hysteroscopic removal, and rarely they contain hyperplasia or carcinoma.
whyNot: A leiomyoma is a clonal smooth muscle tumor that arises from the myometrium. A submucosal one would distort the muscle layer and is usually hypoechoic.
Correct.
Endometrial tissue within the myometrium is adenomyosis, which causes her diffuse enlargement but does not form a mass in the cavity.
Retained placental tissue follows a recent pregnancy or delivery. Her deliveries were years ago.

topics: Structural causes of abnormal uterine bleeding

case: A 13-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of lower abdominal pain for 2 days and inability to urinate for 8 hours. She has had similar cramping pain lasting several days each month for the past 4 months. She has never had a menstrual period. Breast development began at age 10. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. Breasts and pubic hair are Tanner stage 4. A tender suprapubic mass is palpable. Examination of the external genitalia shows a tense, bulging, bluish membrane at the vaginal opening. Ultrasonography shows a vagina distended with echogenic fluid, a normal uterus, and normal ovaries. Diagnosis: imperforate hymen with hematocolpos.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why this patient's symptoms began only in the past 4 months?
options: Mucus secretion accumulating behind the membrane since infancy
Menstrual blood trapped behind the membrane since menarche
Labial adhesions forming after the onset of puberty
Infection of a congenital cyst in the vaginal wall
approach: The hymen is a thin membrane where the vaginal plate meets the urogenital sinus, and it normally perforates before birth.
If it stays closed, it blocks nothing until there is fluid to drain.
At menarche, shed endometrium and blood collect in the vagina (hematocolpos), which causes cyclic pain, a bluish bulge, and possible urinary retention from pressure on the urethra.
questions.why: An imperforate hymen is present from birth, but it usually causes no symptoms in childhood because little fluid forms above it. Once menstruation begins, each period adds blood that cannot escape. The vagina distends into a hematocolpos, which causes monthly cramping pain, a tense bluish membrane at the vaginal opening, and a pelvic mass that can compress the urethra and cause retention. The girl appears to have primary amenorrhea even though she is menstruating.
whyNot: Mucus can collect above an imperforate hymen in a newborn exposed to maternal estrogen (mucocolpos), but it would have appeared in infancy, and the bluish color here reflects blood.
Correct.
Labial adhesions occur in prepubertal girls with low estrogen and tend to resolve as estrogen rises at puberty. They do not form a bulging bluish membrane.
A vaginal wall cyst would not explain monthly cyclic pain beginning at the expected age of menarche, or the absence of menses.

questions.stem: Her first menstrual bleeding most likely began behind the membrane about 4 months ago. In the usual female sequence of puberty, when did her peak height velocity most likely occur?
options: About 1 year before menarche
At the time of menarche
About 1 year after menarche
About 2 years after menarche
approach: Puberty starts when pulsatile GnRH secretion resumes, first as LH pulses during sleep.
In girls the usual order is thelarche, pubarche, growth spurt (peak height velocity), then menarche.
Her first bleed was about 4 months ago, so her fastest growth most likely came about a year before that.
questions.why: Rising estradiol in early puberty drives breast development and, together with growth hormone, the growth spurt. Girls reach peak height velocity early in puberty, usually at Tanner stage 2 to 3 and about 1 year before menarche. After menarche, growth slows, and most girls gain only about 5 to 7 cm more as estrogen closes the growth plates. Boys reach peak height velocity later in puberty than girls.
whyNot: Correct.
Menarche comes after peak height velocity, when growth is already slowing.
Growth slows after menarche as estrogen closes the growth plates.
Most girls are near their final height 2 years after menarche.

questions.stem: Incision of the membrane drains 450 mL of dark blood. The membrane lies within which of the following regions of the perineum?
options: Anal triangle, between the sacrotuberous ligaments
Ischioanal fossa, lateral to the levator ani
Urogenital triangle, between the ischiopubic rami
Pelvic cavity, above the levator ani
approach: The perineum is a diamond bounded by the pubic symphysis, ischiopubic rami, ischial tuberosities, sacrotuberous ligaments, and coccyx.
A line between the ischial tuberosities divides it into the urogenital triangle in front and the anal triangle behind.
The vaginal opening and hymen lie in the vestibule, in the urogenital triangle between the ischiopubic rami.
questions.why: The perineum is the diamond-shaped region below the pelvic floor. Its anterior part, the urogenital triangle, lies between the pubic symphysis and the ischiopubic rami and contains the external genitalia, the vestibule, and the openings of the urethra and vagina. The hymen sits at the vaginal opening in this triangle. The posterior part, the anal triangle, lies between the ischial tuberosities, sacrotuberous ligaments, and coccyx and contains the anal canal.
whyNot: The anal triangle, behind the line between the ischial tuberosities and bounded by the sacrotuberous ligaments, contains the anal canal and ischioanal fossae.
The ischioanal fossae are fat-filled spaces beside the anal canal, in the anal triangle.
Correct.
The pelvic cavity lies above the pelvic floor. The hymen lies below it at the vaginal opening.

questions.stem: Her 17-year-old cousin has cyclic pelvic pain. Imaging shows two separate uterine bodies, two cervices, and a longitudinal vaginal septum. Which of the following developmental errors best explains the cousin's anatomy?
options: Failure of the vaginal plate to canalize
Failure to resorb the midline septum after fusion
Partial fusion of the upper paramesonephric ducts
Complete failure of paramesonephric duct fusion
approach: Paired paramesonephric ducts form the uterine tubes, and their fused lower parts form the uterus, cervix, and upper vagina.
The lower parts fuse first, and the midline wall between them is then resorbed.
Two separate uteri and two cervices mean the ducts never fused (uterus didelphys).
questions.why: The paramesonephric (Mullerian) ducts fuse in the midline to form a single uterus, cervix, and upper vagina, and the wall between them is then resorbed. If the ducts do not fuse at all, each forms its own uterus and cervix, often with a longitudinal vaginal septum, which is uterus didelphys. Partial fusion of the upper ducts gives a bicornuate uterus with two horns and one cervix. Complete fusion with failed resorption of the wall gives a septate uterus with a normal outer contour.
whyNot: Failure of the vaginal plate to canalize gives a transverse vaginal septum or vaginal atresia, with a single uterus.
Failure to resorb the septum gives a septate uterus, which has a single outer uterine contour.
Partial fusion gives a bicornuate uterus, with two horns joined above a single cervix.
Correct.

case: A 17-year-old boy is brought to the physician because he has not gone through puberty. He has never been able to smell. He had an orchiopexy for a right undescended testis at age 2. Height is 178 cm, and arm span is 186 cm. He has no facial or axillary hair. Pubic hair and genitalia are Tanner stage 1, and each testis measures 2 mL (adult 15 to 25). He cannot identify common odors. Serum LH is 0.4 mIU/mL (adult 1.5 to 9.3), FSH is 0.6 mIU/mL (adult 1.4 to 18.1), and testosterone is 22 ng/dL (adult 300 to 1000). MRI shows absent olfactory bulbs and a normal pituitary gland. Diagnosis: Kallmann syndrome (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia).

questions.stem: He receives testosterone injections for 1 year. His libido, muscle mass, and facial hair increase, but his testes remain small, and a semen analysis shows no sperm. Which of the following best explains the absent sperm production?
options: Aromatization of injected testosterone in the tubules
Germ cell destruction by supraphysiologic androgen levels
Antibodies formed against the injected testosterone
No FSH and too little testosterone inside the tubules
approach: Spermatogenesis needs FSH acting on Sertoli cells and a testosterone level inside the tubules far higher than in blood, which requires LH stimulation of Leydig cells.
Injected testosterone raises serum levels enough to virilize but does not create the high intratesticular level.
It also feeds back on the hypothalamus and pituitary and further suppresses any LH and FSH.
questions.why: In the normal male axis, LH drives Leydig cells to make testosterone, which builds up in the testis at levels many times higher than in blood. FSH acts on Sertoli cells to make androgen-binding protein, which holds that testosterone in the tubules, and inhibin B, which feeds back on FSH. Testosterone feeds back on GnRH and LH. In Kallmann syndrome, LH and FSH are absent. Injected testosterone virilizes the body but cannot reproduce the intratesticular level or replace FSH. To start spermatogenesis, men with this condition are treated with hCG, which acts like LH, together with FSH, or with pulsatile GnRH.
whyNot: Some testosterone is converted to estradiol, but this does not explain absent sperm. The problem is missing gonadotropin stimulation.
Replacement doses do not destroy germ cells. The germ cells are simply not stimulated.
Testosterone is a small steroid that does not provoke antibody formation.
Correct.

questions.stem: Male infertility is classified as pretesticular, testicular, or post-testicular. Which of the following best classifies this patient's infertility and gives the reason?
options: Testicular, because Leydig cells make little testosterone
Pretesticular, because the gonadotropin signal is missing
Testicular, because the seminiferous tubules are small
Post-testicular, because the ejaculate lacks sperm
approach: Find the first defect: the hypothalamus fails to release GnRH, so LH and FSH are low.
The testes are small because they are unstimulated; with hCG and FSH they can make testosterone and sperm.
A primary testicular cause would raise LH and FSH, and an obstruction would leave hormone levels normal.
questions.why: Pretesticular causes are hormonal problems outside the testis, chiefly hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, as in Kallmann syndrome, pituitary disease, or hyperprolactinemia. Testicular causes damage the testis itself, such as Klinefelter syndrome, cryptorchidism, varicocele, or mumps orchitis, and they raise FSH and often LH. Post-testicular causes block sperm transport, such as congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens in cystic fibrosis. In this patient, low LH and FSH show the testes are understimulated, so the problem is pretesticular and can be treated with gonadotropins.
whyNot: Low testosterone here follows from absent LH. In primary Leydig cell failure, LH would be high.
Correct.
The tubules are small because FSH and testosterone are lacking. A primary tubular disorder would raise FSH.
Absent sperm in the ejaculate can occur in any category. Post-testicular causes have normal hormone levels and normal sperm production.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy with Crohn disease of the small intestine also has delayed puberty and small testes. He has a scaly, red rash around the mouth and anus, patchy hair loss, poor wound healing, and a reduced sense of taste. Deficiency of which of the following nutrients best explains his findings?
options: Copper
Niacin
Zinc
Selenium
approach: Collect the pattern: dermatitis around the mouth and anus, hair loss, poor wound healing, and reduced taste.
That pattern is zinc deficiency, a risk with small-bowel disease and malabsorption.
Zinc is needed for testicular development and testosterone production, so deficiency causes hypogonadism and delayed sexual maturation.
questions.why: Zinc is a cofactor for many enzymes and a structural part of zinc finger transcription factors, and it is needed for growth, wound healing, taste, and gonadal function. Deficiency from poor intake, malabsorption, or the inherited absorption defect acrodermatitis enteropathica causes dermatitis around the mouth, anus, and extremities, hair loss, impaired taste, poor wound healing, growth delay, and hypogonadism with delayed puberty. Zinc deficiency should be considered in delayed puberty with chronic small-bowel disease.
whyNot: Copper deficiency causes anemia, neutropenia, and a spinal cord disorder resembling vitamin B12 deficiency.
Niacin deficiency (pellagra) causes dermatitis on sun-exposed skin, diarrhea, and dementia. It does not cause periorificial dermatitis or hypogonadism.
Correct.
Selenium deficiency causes cardiomyopathy (Keshan disease) and muscle weakness.

questions.stem: His friend, a 28-year-old man who had bilateral cryptorchidism corrected at age 9, has normal virilization and no sperm in his semen. Which of the following sets of serum findings is most likely in the friend?
options: High FSH, low inhibin B, normal testosterone
Low FSH, low inhibin B, low testosterone
Normal FSH, normal inhibin B, normal testosterone
Low FSH, high inhibin B, high testosterone
approach: Undescended testes sit at core body temperature, which injures germ cells and Sertoli cell function more than Leydig cells.
Damaged Sertoli cells make less inhibin B, so FSH rises from loss of feedback.
Leydig cells usually keep making testosterone, so virilization is preserved.
questions.why: Spermatogenesis needs a temperature about 2 to 3 °C (3.6 to 5.4 °F) below core body temperature. Testes that stay in the inguinal canal or abdomen, especially when correction is late, lose germ cells and Sertoli cell function. Inhibin B falls, and FSH rises because it is no longer held down. Leydig cells tolerate heat better, so testosterone and secondary sex characteristics are usually preserved. This contrasts with Kallmann syndrome, in which all of these values are low. Cryptorchid testes also keep a higher risk of germ cell tumors after orchiopexy.
whyNot: Correct.
Low FSH, inhibin B, and testosterone together point to a pretesticular cause such as this patient's Kallmann syndrome.
Normal values with no sperm suggest an obstruction, such as absence of the vas deferens.
High testosterone with suppressed FSH suggests anabolic steroid use or an androgen-secreting tumor. High inhibin B would not occur with damaged tubules.

dx: Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens in a man with cystic fibrosis
case: A 32-year-old man comes to the physician because he and his wife have been unable to conceive for 2 years. He was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at age 24 during evaluation of nasal polyps and recurrent sinusitis; genetic testing showed a severe CFTR variant (F508del) on one allele and a mild variant on the other. He has normal pulmonary function and no history of pancreatitis. Each testis measures 20 mL (15 to 25), and the vas deferens cannot be palpated on either side of the scrotum. Serum LH, FSH, and testosterone are within the reference ranges. Two semen analyses show no sperm. Diagnosis: congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens in a man with cystic fibrosis.

questions.stem: A testicular biopsy shows normal spermatogenesis, and sperm are to be retrieved surgically for assisted reproduction. Which of the following is the most distal structure along the normal sperm pathway from which sperm can most likely be retrieved in this patient?
options: Head of the epididymis
Ejaculatory duct
Prostatic urethra
Ampulla of the ductus deferens
approach: Trace sperm: seminiferous tubules, rete testis, efferent ductules, epididymis, ductus deferens, ejaculatory duct, then the prostatic, membranous, and spongy urethra.
In this condition the ductus deferens is missing on both sides, and the body and tail of the epididymis are often missing too.
Sperm collect in the remaining epididymal head, the most distal site before the gap, so they are aspirated there.
questions.why: Sperm leave the seminiferous tubules, pass through the rete testis and efferent ductules into the head of the epididymis, and mature as they move through its body and tail. From the tail they enter the ductus deferens, which joins the duct of the seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct, which opens into the prostatic urethra. In congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens, the path is interrupted, so normally made sperm never reach the ejaculatory duct or urethra. They collect in the epididymis and can be aspirated from it, or extracted from the testis, for in vitro fertilization with intracytoplasmic sperm injection.
whyNot: Correct.
The ejaculatory duct lies beyond the missing ductus deferens, so sperm cannot reach it.
The prostatic urethra lies beyond the missing segment and receives no sperm in this patient.
The ampulla is the dilated end of the ductus deferens, which is absent in this patient.

questions.stem: Each of his semen samples has a volume of 0.7 mL (1.4 or more) and a pH of 6.6 (7.2 or more), and the samples do not coagulate after ejaculation. Which of the following additional findings in the seminal fluid is most likely?
options: Low prostate-specific antigen
Low citrate
Low zinc
Low fructose
approach: Seminal vesicles supply most of the semen volume as alkaline fluid with fructose and semenogelin, the protein that forms the coagulum.
In this condition the seminal vesicles are absent or underdeveloped, so the ejaculate lacks their fluid.
The small, acidic, noncoagulating sample is mostly prostatic fluid, which still contains PSA, citrate, and zinc but little fructose.
questions.why: About two thirds of semen volume comes from the seminal vesicles: alkaline fluid rich in fructose, which fuels sperm, and semenogelin, which forms the clot after ejaculation. The prostate adds about a quarter to a third: slightly acidic fluid with citrate, zinc, and prostate-specific antigen (PSA), a serine protease that later liquefies the clot. When the seminal vesicles are missing or blocked, semen is low in volume, acidic, does not coagulate, and has low or absent fructose. Prostatic products remain.
whyNot: PSA comes from the prostate, which is normal in this patient, so it is still present in the fluid.
Citrate is a prostatic product and remains in the fluid.
Zinc is concentrated by the prostate and remains in the fluid.
Correct.

questions.stem: Sperm aspirated from his epididymis are motile. Before conventional in vitro fertilization, they are incubated for several hours in a medium that mimics the female reproductive tract so that they can undergo the acrosome reaction at the zona pellucida. Which of the following changes does this incubation produce?
options: Formation of the acrosome from the Golgi apparatus
Loss of membrane cholesterol and surface glycoproteins
Shedding of excess cytoplasm as a residual body
Acquisition of forward motility in the epididymal duct
approach: Sort the events by place and time: spermiogenesis in the testis, maturation and motility in the epididymis, capacitation in the female tract.
Capacitation removes cholesterol and coating glycoproteins from the membrane over the sperm head, which raises its fluidity and calcium entry.
Only capacitated sperm can undergo the acrosome reaction when they bind the zona pellucida.
questions.why: Ejaculated or aspirated sperm cannot fertilize at once. In the female tract, mainly the uterus and uterine tube, they undergo capacitation over several hours as albumin and other factors strip cholesterol and seminal glycoproteins from the plasma membrane over the acrosome. The membrane becomes more fluid, calcium enters, and motility becomes hyperactivated. When a capacitated sperm binds the zona pellucida, the acrosome releases enzymes such as acrosin that let it pass through the zona. Laboratories reproduce capacitation in culture media before conventional in vitro fertilization.
whyNot: The acrosome forms from Golgi vesicles during spermiogenesis in the testis, long before ejaculation.
Correct.
Excess cytoplasm is shed as a residual body during spermiogenesis, and Sertoli cells phagocytose it.
Sperm gain forward motility while passing through the epididymis. These sperm are already motile, and the incubation changes their membrane.

questions.stem: The structure that is absent on both sides in this patient develops from which of the following embryonic structures, under the influence of which hormone?
options: Paramesonephric duct, stimulated by testosterone
Mesonephric duct, stimulated by dihydrotestosterone
Mesonephric duct, stimulated by testosterone
Urogenital sinus, stimulated by dihydrotestosterone
approach: The ductus deferens, epididymis, seminal vesicle, and ejaculatory duct come from the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct.
Testosterone from fetal Leydig cells maintains and differentiates the mesonephric duct directly, without conversion to DHT.
DHT masculinizes the prostate and external genitalia, and Sertoli cell anti-Mullerian hormone makes the paramesonephric ducts regress.
questions.why: In a male fetus, Sertoli cells secrete anti-Mullerian hormone, which makes the paramesonephric ducts regress. Leydig cells secrete testosterone, which acts on the mesonephric ducts to form the epididymis, ductus deferens, seminal vesicles, and ejaculatory ducts. 5-alpha-reductase converts testosterone to DHT in the urogenital sinus and genital tubercle, which form the prostate, penis, and scrotum. In cystic fibrosis, the hormones are normal, as in this patient; the mesonephric derivatives are thought to fail or degenerate because abnormal CFTR function leaves thick secretions in the developing ducts.
whyNot: The paramesonephric (Mullerian) ducts form the uterine tubes, uterus, cervix, and upper vagina. In males they regress under anti-Mullerian hormone.
The mesonephric duct is the right origin, but it responds to testosterone itself. Men with 5-alpha-reductase deficiency still form a normal ductus deferens.
Correct.
The urogenital sinus forms the prostate, bladder, and urethra under DHT. It does not form the ductus deferens.

dx: Penile fracture (rupture of the tunica albuginea)
case: A 38-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after he heard a popping sound during sexual intercourse when his erect penis struck his partner's pubic bone. He had immediate severe pain and loss of erection, followed by rapid swelling. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 138/84 mm Hg. The penile shaft is swollen and purple and deviates to the right. A tender defect is palpable on the left lateral shaft. There is no blood at the urethral meatus, and he voids normally. Ultrasonography shows a 1-cm tear in the tunica albuginea of the left corpus cavernosum with an adjacent hematoma. Diagnosis: penile fracture.

questions.stem: If this patient had also had blood at the urethral meatus and difficulty voiding, which of the following structures would most likely also have been torn?
options: Contralateral corpus cavernosum
Deep dorsal vein of the penis
Corpus spongiosum
Ischiocavernosus muscle
approach: The shaft has three erectile bodies: paired dorsal corpora cavernosa and a single ventral corpus spongiosum.
Each is wrapped in tunica albuginea, and the spongy urethra runs within the corpus spongiosum.
Blood at the meatus and trouble voiding mean the tear extended into the corpus spongiosum and urethra.
questions.why: The corpora cavernosa lie side by side in the dorsal shaft, each enclosed by a thick tunica albuginea. The corpus spongiosum lies ventrally in the groove between them, surrounds the spongy urethra, and expands distally as the glans. In a penile fracture the tunica albuginea of a corpus cavernosum tears while the penis is rigid. In a minority of cases the tear extends into the corpus spongiosum and urethra, which gives blood at the meatus, painful voiding, or urinary retention.
whyNot: Both corpora cavernosa can tear in severe injuries, but neither carries the urethra.
Rupture of the deep dorsal vein can mimic a fracture with swelling and bruising, but it does not involve the urethra.
Correct.
The ischiocavernosus muscle covers the crura in the perineum and does not contain the urethra.

questions.stem: Which of the following sequences produced the high pressure in his corpora cavernosa at the time of injury?
options: NO raises cGMP; trabecular muscle relaxes; venules are compressed
NO raises cAMP; trabecular muscle contracts; arteries dilate
Norepinephrine raises cGMP; trabecular muscle relaxes; veins dilate
Acetylcholine raises IP3; trabecular muscle contracts; venules close
approach: Parasympathetic nerves and endothelium release nitric oxide (NO) in the corpora.
NO activates guanylyl cyclase, cGMP rises, and cavernosal and arterial smooth muscle relaxes.
Sinusoids fill with arterial blood and press the venules beneath the tunica albuginea against it, which traps blood and raises pressure.
questions.why: Erection starts with NO released from parasympathetic nerve endings and from endothelium. NO activates soluble guanylyl cyclase, and cGMP lowers intracellular calcium, so the trabecular and arterial smooth muscle relaxes. Arterial inflow fills the sinusoids, which expand and compress the venules between them and the tunica albuginea, which limits outflow. Pressure in the corpora approaches arterial pressure and rises further when the ischiocavernosus muscles contract. The stretched, thinned tunica can then tear under a sudden bending force.
whyNot: Correct.
NO acts through cGMP, and erection requires smooth muscle relaxation.
Norepinephrine from sympathetic nerves contracts cavernosal smooth muscle and causes loss of erection.
Smooth muscle contraction through IP3 and calcium empties the sinusoids and ends erection.

questions.stem: His uncle had a radical prostatectomy 6 months ago. The uncle now cannot achieve an erection, although sensation of the penile skin is normal. Injury to fibers from which of the following sources best explains the uncle's erectile dysfunction?
options: Pudendal nerve from S2 to S4
Sympathetic hypogastric nerves from T11 to L2
Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve, L1 and L2
Pelvic splanchnic nerves from S2 to S4
approach: Separate the nerves of the male sexual response: erection is parasympathetic, emission sympathetic, and ejaculation somatic.
Parasympathetic fibers from S2 to S4 run as the pelvic splanchnic nerves into the pelvic plexus and continue as the cavernous nerves beside the prostate.
Prostatectomy can injure the cavernous nerves while sparing the pudendal nerve, which carries penile skin sensation.
questions.why: Erection depends on parasympathetic fibers from S2 to S4. They leave as the pelvic splanchnic nerves, join the inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexus, and reach the corpora as the cavernous nerves, which run along the posterolateral prostate. Their release of NO starts erection. Radical prostatectomy can injure these nerves, so erection fails while the pudendal nerve, which carries skin sensation and drives ejaculation, remains intact. Sympathetic fibers from T11 to L2 cause emission.
whyNot: The pudendal nerve carries penile skin sensation, which is intact, and drives the bulbospongiosus and ischiocavernosus muscles during ejaculation.
Sympathetic fibers in the hypogastric nerves cause emission by contracting the ductus deferens, seminal vesicles, and prostate. Their loss impairs emission.
The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve supplies the cremaster muscle and anterior scrotal skin. It does not control erection.
Correct.

topics: Innervation of the male sexual response

questions.stem: Eight months after surgical repair, he has a firm, nontender plaque at the repair site on the left lateral shaft, and his penis now bends during erection. Toward which of the following directions does his penis most likely bend during erection?
options: Dorsally, away from the urethra
Toward the left side
Toward the right side
Ventrally, toward the urethra
approach: A fibrous plaque in the tunica albuginea, as in Peyronie disease, does not stretch during erection.
The normal tunica on the opposite side lengthens while the plaque side stays short.
The penis therefore bends toward the side of the plaque, here the left.
questions.why: Peyronie disease is a fibrous plaque in the tunica albuginea, usually from repeated minor injury and abnormal healing. A scar after repair of a penile fracture behaves the same way. During erection the elastic tunica elsewhere expands, but the plaque does not, so that side stays shorter and the shaft curves toward it. Most plaques of Peyronie disease are dorsal and cause upward curvature, while this lateral scar bends the penis to the left. Plaques can also cause painful erections and erectile dysfunction.
whyNot: Dorsal curvature occurs with dorsal plaques, the most common site in Peyronie disease. His plaque is lateral.
Correct.
His penis deviated to the right at the time of injury because the hematoma pushed it away from the tear. A healed, inelastic scar on the left bends it toward the left.
Ventral curvature occurs with ventral plaques or with chordee in hypospadias.
